You Answer 8 Out of 10 Right. The Exam Still Beats You.

Eight out of ten SSC CGL aspirants can recite the basic question tag rule in their sleep. Positive statement, negative tag. Negative statement, positive tag. Then the exam hands them 'Nobody objected, did he?' or 'I am late, isn't I?' and the confidence disappears in half a second. Question tags don't fail you because you don't know the rule — they fail you because the exam is built entirely around the five exceptions nobody drills properly.

Quick Answer: A question tag repeats the main clause's auxiliary verb, reverses its polarity, and matches the subject with the correct pronoun. Five fixed forms — aren't I, shall we, didn't (for used to), isn't/aren't there, and they (for nobody/everybody/someone) — account for the majority of tag errors in SSC CGL and Bank PO exams. Mastering these five plus the polarity rule closes almost every gap.

Why Question Tags Keep Beating Strong Students

Here's the part nobody explains properly: question tags aren't tested to check if you know the rule. They're tested to check if you can apply the rule under pressure, inside a sentence built specifically to hide the trap. Every wrong answer choice in an SSC or Bank PO tag question is designed around one specific blind spot.

  • You apply the polarity rule correctly, but miss that 'hardly', 'never', or 'seldom' already made the sentence negative — so you flip the tag the wrong way.
  • You freeze on 'I am' and default to 'amn't I' or 'isn't I', both of which are always wrong in standard exam English.
  • You keep the polarity the same after 'Let's', because 'shall we' doesn't feel like it 'matches' anything you were taught.
  • You match the verb correctly but use 'he' or 'she' for 'nobody', 'everybody', or 'someone' instead of the required 'they'.
  • You second-guess a correct tag because it sounds unnatural compared to how it's said in spoken Indian English.

I know exactly how this feels. Students walk out of the exam hall, replay the sentence in their head, and realize the mistake thirty seconds too late — every single batch, every single year. But here's what most people get wrong: they keep collecting more example sentences instead of locking the small, fixed list of exceptions that actually decides the outcome.

5 Mistakes That Repeat Every Single Year

1. Matching polarity instead of reversing it.
A positive statement always needs a negative tag, and a negative statement always needs a positive one. Exams bury this rule inside long, distracting sentences so your eye catches the wrong cue.
Wrong: Your eldest sister lives in a big city, does she?
Correct: Your eldest sister lives in a big city, doesn't she?
SSC CGL Exam Pattern

2. Reaching for 'isn't/wasn't' when no auxiliary is visible.
When the main clause is in simple present or simple past with no helping verb, the tag must use do/does/did — never isn't or wasn't.
Wrong: Every Saturday, your mother prepares a pudding, isn't she?
Correct: Every Saturday, your mother prepares a pudding, doesn't she?
SSC CGL Exam Pattern

3. Defaulting to 'isn't it' for every modal sentence.
The tag must repeat the exact modal used in the statement — should, could, would, must — never a generic 'isn't it'.
Wrong: It should be started early, isn't it?
Correct: It should be started early, shouldn't it?
Bank PO Exam Pattern

4. Inventing a tag for 'I am'.
Standard English has exactly one accepted tag for 'I am', and it breaks the usual pattern on purpose.
Wrong: I am late, amn't I? / isn't I?
Correct: I am late, aren't I?

5. Guessing on 'Let's' and indefinite pronouns.
'Let's' always takes 'shall we', with no exceptions. Nobody, everybody, and someone always take 'they' in the tag, regardless of gender.
Wrong: Let's start the meeting, will we? / Nobody came, did he?
Correct: Let's start the meeting, shall we? / Nobody came, did they?

The 7-Step System for a Perfect Tag Every Time

You don't need to memorize twenty separate rules. You need one fixed sequence you can run through in under twenty seconds, every single time.

Step 1: Scan for hidden negatives first. Words like not, never, hardly, seldom, rarely, no one, and nobody already make the statement negative — even without the word 'not' appearing anywhere near the tag position. If any of these is present, the tag must be positive.

❌ He never comes late, doesn't he?
✅ He never comes late, does he?

Step 2: Locate the auxiliary or modal in the main clause. is, are, was, were, have, has, had, will, would, can, could, should, must — repeat that exact word in the tag, unchanged except for polarity.

Step 3: If no auxiliary is visible, supply do/does/did. Match it to the tense and the person of the subject — never insert a helping verb that wasn't implied by the sentence.

❌ She writes novels, isn't she?
✅ She writes novels, doesn't she?

Step 4: Convert the subject to the correct pronoun. He/she/it stays as is; nouns become he/she/it/they based on number; nobody, everybody, anyone, and someone all become 'they'; there stays as 'there'.

Step 5: Lock the five fixed exceptions cold. I am → aren't I. Let's → shall we. Used to → didn't. There is/are → isn't/aren't there. An imperative like 'Open the door' → will you / won't you.

❌ He used to smoke, usedn't he?
✅ He used to smoke, didn't he?

Step 6: Never let the main verb slip into the tag. The tag is only auxiliary + pronoun + question mark — nothing else.

❌ He runs fast, doesn't he run?
✅ He runs fast, doesn't he?

Step 7: Re-read the whole sentence before locking your answer. A large share of wrong answers come from students who spot the first odd word and mark it, missing a genuine polarity error hiding later in the same sentence.

How Rahul Went From 3 Wrong to Zero Wrong

Rahul, an SSC CGL aspirant from Pune, was losing two to three marks on nearly every mock test purely on question-tag questions — not because he didn't know the polarity rule, but because 'I am', 'Let's', and 'nobody' kept catching him off guard under time pressure. For three weeks, he wrote only the five fixed exceptions on a single flashcard and reviewed it before every mock, without adding a single new example sentence. Tag-related errors in his mocks dropped to zero within that period. Nothing else in his preparation changed — just the shift from chasing endless examples to locking five fixed forms. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From 15+ Years of Coaching

  • Underline every negative word before you touch the tag. Hardly, never, seldom, rarely, no, and nobody decide the polarity before you even reach the comma.
  • Treat 'I am' and 'Let's' as fixed formulas, not calculations. The instant you see them, write 'aren't I' or 'shall we' automatically — don't reason it out mid-exam.
  • Practise only sentence formats that mirror real exam length. Short, textbook-style example sentences build false confidence; the actual exam always hides the tag inside a longer, more distracting clause.
  • Never trust how the sentence 'sounds' in spoken Indian English. 'Isn't it' gets used for everything in casual speech, but the exam accepts only the grammatically exact tag — your ear is not a reliable judge here.

The Bottom Line

Question tags stop costing marks the moment you stop treating them as twenty scattered rules and start running one fixed sequence: check for hidden negatives, find the auxiliary, match the pronoun, lock the five exceptions, keep the main verb out, and re-read before you answer. That sequence, paired with the five fixed forms, turns question tags from a guessing game into one of the most reliable, predictable mark-scoring sections in SSC CGL and Bank PO.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1. What is the single most common question tag mistake in SSC CGL?
Keeping the same polarity instead of reversing it, and using 'isn't/wasn't' instead of do/does/did when no auxiliary is present in the main clause.
Q2. Is 'aren't I' really the only correct tag for 'I am'?
Yes. Both 'amn't I' and 'isn't I' are considered incorrect in standard exam English; 'aren't I' is the only accepted fixed form.
Q3. What tag follows 'Let's'?
Always 'shall we'. Forms like 'will we' or 'won't we' are incorrect after 'Let's' in every case.
Q4. Do words like 'hardly' and 'never' change the required tag?
Yes. These words make the statement negative on their own, so the question tag that follows must be positive.
Q5. I already know the basic question tag rule — is this guide still useful?
Yes. Most aspirants already know the basic rule; what costs marks is the five fixed exceptions and hidden-negative sentences, which this guide focuses on specifically.
Q6. Do these rules apply to IBPS PO and Railway exams as well?
Yes. Question tag patterns overlap heavily across SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB, and similar competitive English papers.
Q7. How is 'there is/are' handled in a question tag?
'There' is treated as the subject and repeated in the tag as 'isn't there' or 'aren't there', matching the singular or plural form used in the statement.
Q8. Why do imperative sentences take 'will you' as a tag?
Imperative sentences (commands or requests) don't have a visible subject or auxiliary, so English grammar assigns them the fixed tag 'will you' or 'won't you' by convention.
